title: The Day Death Died
summary: This part teaches how to read the Bible by distinguishing its natural and heavenly perspectives: Matthew, Mark and Luke record what Jesus was seen to do, while John and Revelation give heaven’s view of the same events. Reading Luke 3, the preacher argues that John the Baptist heralded not wrath but the “remission” of sin, the removal of everything creation was never meant to be, accomplished through a simultaneous baptism of Spirit and fire at the cross. Revelation 20:11–15 is then read as heaven’s view of the crucifixion: the dead are judged by the books of the tree of knowledge, Death and Hades are destroyed, and (on his reading of the Greek) “anything” not in the Book of Life, not “anyone,” is burned. The part closes with the woman at the well, presented as a woman unloved by five husbands whom Jesus refuses to see according to the record in the books.
thesis: At the cross the baptism of Spirit and fire gave humanity everything it needs and burned every record, power and identity that stood against it, so death, Hades and the condemning books are already destroyed.

flow.text: Scripture holds natural and supernatural perspectives that often run parallel, as with Abraham’s natural (sand) and spiritual (stars) descendants.
Matthew, Mark and Luke record what was seen and heard; John and Revelation give heaven’s revelatory view. John 1 is presented as heaven’s parallel and correction to Genesis.
Luke 3 shows John preaching the “remission” of sins: the Lamb would take away creation’s distorted form, a second act of creation spoken through the Son.
John’s rebuke of the crowd is read as rejecting fear of coming wrath; repentance means bearing the fruit of a new mind, shown in generous and honest living.
Jesus comes with an axe for the tree of knowledge and baptizes in Spirit and fire, both happening at the cross: one supplies everything, the other burns away what was never meant to be.
Revelation is a third‑heaven view of history and a record of the finished work, so Rev 20:11–15 is read as heaven’s side of the crucifixion.
With volunteers as the dead, the books, the Book of Life, and Death and Hades, the scene shows humanity judged by the books, then released as Death and Hades are cast into the fire.
The preacher claims the Greek means “anything”, so the books, the tree’s record and every false identity burn, not people.
People die because they strive to rewrite the books; the only response is to recognize that death, Hades, the books and the tree are gone.
John the Baptist is the greatest of the prophets because he alone could point and say the Coming One is here.
John 4 shows how Jesus refuses to see a person by the record of the books: He knows her history and still offers living water.
Everything you were never meant to be was cast into the fire so you can step into everything you were made for.

teachings.title: The Bible misused is not the Bible at fault
teachings.body: Most problems in the church come from a wrong view of Scripture, not from Scripture itself. Using the Bible to beat sinners instead of freeing them does not make the book the problem.

teachings.title: Natural and heavenly perspectives
teachings.body: The Bible contains natural and heavenly things, and they often describe the same events from different angles. Abraham was promised descendants like the sand (his natural line) and like the stars (everyone who comes into Christ).

teachings.title: Synoptics natural, John and Revelation supernatural
teachings.body: Matthew, Mark and Luke recorded what they saw and heard Jesus do. John was the first Gospel writer to add revelatory information, and Revelation likewise gives heaven’s perspective on what the Gospels show on earth. How you read Revelation decides whether you fear the future or know humanity’s enemies are already defeated.

teachings.title: John 1 as heaven’s Genesis
teachings.body: John 1:1 is described as the correction to Genesis: the two are accounts of the same beginning, one from heaven’s view and one from Moses’ view.

teachings.title: Remission means removal of the distorted form
teachings.body: John preached a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins. The preacher says the word (which he gives as aphiēmi) means taking away the distorted form from who you are; it is the same word translated “forgiveness.” So John’s message was not religious or punitive but about removing what we were never meant to be.

teachings.title: John was heralding what Jesus would do
teachings.body: John’s Jordan baptism itself was not that remission; he was announcing how the Lamb would take away the sin of the world. The Coming One would remove creation’s distorted form, everything it was never meant to be.

teachings.title: Creation 2.0
teachings.body: Isaiah’s picture of valleys filled and crooked places straightened announces someone coming to fix everything. As in Genesis, God sees something dark and formless and speaks; this time He speaks through His Son to undo the distortion.

teachings.title: “Who warned you to flee wrath?” — wrong message
teachings.body: John’s rebuke of the crowds is read as saying their focus on fleeing wrath was the wrong message. A wrath‑based message kills; the real message is a new mindset for a new creation.

teachings.title: Repentance as a new mind
teachings.body: Repentance (metanoia) is explained as higher knowledge, the mind of Christ. Bearing fruit worthy of repentance means living out that new mind.

teachings.title: Fruit looks like natural Christlikeness
teachings.body: When the crowd, tax collectors and soldiers ask what to do, John tells them to share clothes and food, take no more than is due, not intimidate or falsely accuse, and be content. This is acting like your true self and stepping into Christ’s identity.

teachings.title: The axe is for the tree
teachings.body: Jesus comes with an axe laid to the root; the tree to be removed is the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and with it the books recorded through that tree. Every tree without good fruit is burned.

teachings.title: Baptism of fire is not mainly an experience
teachings.body: Powerful encounters are real and valuable, but calling them “baptism of fire” can hide what really happened. The baptism of fire happened to all creation 2,000 years ago and removed everything it was never meant to be.

teachings.title: Spirit and fire at the cross simultaneously
teachings.body: John is a revelator giving heaven’s insight into Jesus’ tactic. The baptism of the Spirit gave everything needed for life and godliness; the baptism of fire quenched everything you were never supposed to be. Both happened together at the cross; the wheat is gathered and the chaff burned.

teachings.title: Lamb who takes away the hamartia of the kosmos
teachings.body: John pointed Jesus out as the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world, explained as taking away the world’s distorted form. There was a day death died, and it lies far in your past.

teachings.title: Revelation is the record of the finished work
teachings.body: Revelation is a third‑heaven view of human history and the record of Jesus’ finished work. The preacher avoids labels (preterist, partial preterist, futurist) so hearers don’t box themselves in.

teachings.title: Rev 20 is heaven’s view of the crucifixion
teachings.body: All humanity was taken into Jesus, who became sin; the dead are judged by their works as written in the books, which were written by the tree of knowledge. The sea, Death and Hades give up their dead, so none of them has dominion over any human; then Death and Hades are cast into the lake of fire.

teachings.title: “Anything,” not “anyone”
teachings.body: The preacher says translating “anyone” in Rev 20:15 is a bad translation and the Greek means “anything,” an indefinite pronoun used when the writer won’t list every item. So it is not people but the books and everything not written in the Lamb’s book that burn.

teachings.title: Every false label burned
teachings.body: Hell, death, the grave and the law were taken away from humanity. Your divorce, addiction, shame, anxiety and depression, anything said about you that His book does not say, was cast into the fire. The only book left standing is the one in you.

teachings.title: The body prepared: your incarnation
teachings.body: God did not want sacrifice but prepared a body to do His will, as written in the volume of the book. Your incarnation is ordained, and to step into it the things written in the books had to go: the Book of Life comes in and the books of knowledge of good and evil are burned with the tree.

teachings.title: No record remains
teachings.body: There is no longer any record comparing your performance with the books of heaven; it is removed as far as east from west. The playful line: the sea of forgetfulness was made of fire.

teachings.title: Why we die: trying to rewrite the books
teachings.body: People die because they earn, strive, try and deserve, attempting to rewrite what was written. You cannot rewrite the books; you can only submit to what was written in the Book, and then the books are burned.

teachings.title: John the Baptist the greatest
teachings.body: John’s message was so important he was called the greatest born of women up to his time. The prophets all said “He is coming”; John alone could say “There He is.”

teachings.title: Mechanics of death, burial and resurrection
teachings.body: On earth Jesus takes humanity’s distorted form and its perceived separation from God; in heaven, while the books are being burned, He opens His eyes again. Nothing you offer or sacrifice makes this happen; you only recognize that death, Hades, the books and the tree are gone and only the tree of life and the Book remain.

teachings.title: Jesus needed to go through Samaria
teachings.body: Religious people went around Samaria, but Jesus needed to go through it, which is good news for the outsider.

teachings.title: The woman at the well was not immoral
teachings.body: The common teaching that she was a prostitute or adulteress is rejected. Samaritans were despised because they adopted Jewish culture and law without being in the lineage, and she lived under that religious system.

teachings.title: Divorce certificates and God’s love for women
teachings.body: Moses allowed certificates of divorce because of hard hearts. The preacher explains a certified divorce (a woman unloved by her husband could obtain it and remarry without being killed for lacking a consummation garment) versus a non‑certified divorce for adultery. Women were never meant to be outside the care of a loving man (bride price, preparing a place, next‑of‑kin care); this is not a license but a sign of God’s love.

teachings.title: Jesus as her seventh man
teachings.body: Being alive after five husbands shows none of them loved her, and the current man has made no commitment. Jesus names her history so she will not walk away thinking He offered living water without knowing her; He offers to be the seventh, faithful one who never sees her by the books.

teachings.title: Choose life
teachings.body: We have twisted the message to make people fear the best Father. Like Deuteronomy’s call to choose life, everything you were never meant to be was burned so you can step into everything you were made for.

stories.title: Volunteers act out Revelation 20
stories.text: The preacher has the congregation play “the dead,” another person play the Book of Life, and another play Death and Hades, while “books” are identified. The enactment shows humanity judged by the books, then released, with Death, Hades and the books, not people, going into the fire.

stories.title: Defending the woman at the well
stories.text: The preacher and his wife each had experiences where they felt led to defend the Samaritan woman’s honor against the common view that she was a prostitute. It frames her as a victim of unloving men and religion rather than a sinner.

stories.title: Encounters and the ‘baptism of fire’ label
stories.text: He affirms lightning‑strike encounters with God as real and relevant but suggests calling them something else (being “rocked,” “high on the Most High”), so believers don’t miss that the true baptism of fire already happened at the cross.

stories.title: Reading only the NKJV
stories.text: He preaches from the New King James because after years of reading it he cannot read other versions without mentally correcting them; he listens to paraphrase translations instead. It explains his textual habits.

stories.title: “The sea of forgetfulness was made of fire”
stories.text: A joking T‑shirt line summarising the point: sins are not just forgotten but burned up.

words.claimed: Two parts: apo “away from” + hiēmi “by identity”; removal of the distorted form from who you are; same word as “forgiveness”.
words.lexicon: aphiēmi = apo (away) + hiēmi (to send, throw); meanings: send away, release, let go, cancel a debt, forgive. Luke 3:3 actually uses the noun aphesis (release, pardon, cancellation). Nothing in the root means “by identity”.

words.claimed: Higher knowledge; the mind of Christ.
words.lexicon: A change of mind or purpose, turning about, repentance (meta + noeō, “perceive/think”). It does not mean “higher” knowledge, though it does involve a changed mind.

words.claimed: Distorted form; the world’s distortion from who it is.
words.lexicon: Sin, a wrong, failure; in classical usage missing the mark or error. “Distorted form” is a theological paraphrase, not a lexical meaning.

words.claimed: Creation/the world whose sin is taken away.
words.lexicon: Order, adornment, the world, humanity; in John often the human world alienated from God.

words.claimed: Means “anything,” not “anyone”; a genitive indefinite pronoun used for unnamed things, so things, not people, are cast into the fire.
words.lexicon: tis is the indefinite pronoun “someone, anyone”; the neuter “anything” would be ti. In Rev 20:15 it is masculine/feminine nominative singular (ei tis ouch heurethē … gegrammenos, with a masculine participle), so “anyone/whoever” is correct. It is not genitive here. The definition read aloud resembles a concordance gloss covering all forms of the word.

questions.q: What is the difference between the natural and the heavenly records of Jesus in the series?
questions.a: Matthew, Mark and Luke record what people saw and heard Jesus do. John and Revelation reveal heaven’s perspective on the same events, so Revelation is read as heaven’s view of the cross rather than a fearful forecast.

questions.q: What did John the Baptist mean by the “remission of sins”?
questions.a: The sermon says it means the taking away of the distorted form from who we are. John was heralding the Lamb who would remove everything creation was never meant to be, not threatening punishment.

questions.q: When and what was the baptism of fire, according to this part?
questions.a: It happened to all creation at the cross, alongside the baptism of the Spirit. The Spirit supplied everything needed for life and godliness while the fire burned everything we were never meant to be.

questions.q: How does the preacher read Revelation 20:11–15?
questions.a: As heaven’s view of the crucifixion: humanity, taken into Jesus, is judged by the books of the tree of knowledge, Death and Hades are destroyed, and anything not written in the Lamb’s Book of Life (not people) is burned.

questions.q: Why, according to the sermon, do people still experience death?
questions.a: Because they earn, strive and try to deserve, attempting to rewrite what the books say. The answer is to stop striving and recognize that the books, the tree, death and Hades are gone.

questions.q: Why did Jesus bring up the Samaritan woman’s husbands?
questions.a: Not to expose her but so she would not walk away thinking He did not know her. He knew all five men had put her away and still offered Himself as the faithful one who would never see her by the books.

questions.q: What personal things does the sermon say were cast into the fire?
questions.a: Divorce, addiction, shame, anxiety, depression, and anything said about you that is not said in His book.

practice: Read Scripture distinguishing natural and heavenly perspectives; read Revelation as the finished work, not a source of fear.
Stop striving to earn or deserve; rest in the fact that the condemning books are burned.
Name specific labels (shame, addiction, divorce, anxiety) and recognize them as already cast into the fire.
Live out repentance as a new mind: share with those in need, be honest in work, don’t intimidate, be content.
Value encounters with God without confusing them with the finished baptism of Spirit and fire.
See others, like Jesus saw the Samaritan woman, by the Book of Life rather than their history.
Stop using the Bible to frighten people; present God as the best Father and call people to choose life.

fair.claim: aphiēmi means apo “away from” + hiēmi “by identity,” i.e. removing a distorted form from one’s identity.
fair.note: The root hiēmi means “to send/throw,” so aphiēmi is “send away, release, let go, forgive.” No lexicon (BDAG, LSJ) gives “by identity.” Luke 3:3 actually uses the noun aphesis (release, forgiveness). Charitable reading: “release from” sin is genuinely the idea, and the preacher’s gloss is a theological image of that release.

fair.claim: The Greek word in Rev 20:15 means “anything,” so only books and false identities, not people, are cast into the lake of fire.
fair.note: The Greek is ei tis … gegrammenos: tis is masculine/feminine (the neuter would be ti) and the participle is masculine, so “anyone/whoever” is grammatically required; it is nominative, not genitive. Every major translation, not only the KJV (which reads “whosoever”), renders it as a person. The surrounding verses speak of the dead being judged by their works and of people in the lake of fire (Rev 20:10; 21:8). Charitable reading: some Christian universalist and ‘restorative’ readers hold that the fire ultimately purges rather than torments, but that conclusion is argued theologically, not from this pronoun.

fair.claim: Revelation 20:11–15 (the great white throne) describes what happened at the crucifixion.
fair.note: Most Christian traditions (futurist, historicist, amillennial and most preterist) read the great white throne as the final judgment at the end of the age, after the millennium and the release of Satan. Seeing the cross as the decisive judgment is biblical (John 12:31; Col 2:15), and idealist readings do find the cross behind Revelation’s imagery, but placing Rev 20:11–15 at the cross is a minority view.

fair.claim: The baptism of fire happened to all creation at the cross and is not a personal experience.
fair.note: Commentators usually read Luke 3:16–17 either as the Pentecost outpouring (Acts 2:3, “tongues as of fire”) or as judgment, since in the next verse the chaff is burned and the fruitless tree in Luke 3:9 is cut down. Many also see a purifying fire for believers. Linking it to the cross is unusual, though the cross as the place where judgment fell is a mainstream idea.

fair.claim: John’s “who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?” means wrath was the wrong message.
fair.note: In context John is rebuking hearers who sought baptism without real change; he goes straight on to warn of the axe and of unquenchable fire for chaff (Luke 3:9, 17), and Luke calls this preaching good news (3:18). Most readers therefore see John as affirming coming judgment while offering escape through repentance. Charitable reading: the preacher stresses that John’s heart was release and restoration rather than fear.

fair.claim: John’s Jordan baptism was not itself the baptism for the remission of sins.
fair.note: Luke 3:3 and Mark 1:4 explicitly describe John’s own baptism as “of repentance for the remission of sins.” Many scholars agree it pointed forward to the Messiah, which may be the preacher’s point, but the text does call John’s baptism by that name.

fair.claim: Repentance (metanoia) means higher knowledge; hamartia means distorted form.
fair.note: Metanoia means a change of mind or turning; nothing in it means “higher.” Hamartia means sin, failure or missing the mark. Both glosses are theological paraphrase rather than lexical meaning. Charitable reading: repentance does involve a renewed mind (Rom 12:2), and sin does mar God’s image.

fair.claim: Death died at the cross and is far in our past.
fair.note: Scripture says Christ abolished death and broke its power (2 Tim 1:10; Heb 2:14–15), but also that death is the last enemy still to be destroyed at Christ’s return (1 Cor 15:26, 54–55) and that people still die (Heb 9:27). Mainstream teaching holds death defeated in principle and finally removed at the resurrection. Charitable reading: the preacher speaks of death’s power and sting being broken for the believer.

fair.claim: Matthew, Mark and Luke are only natural records; John and Revelation alone are revelatory, and John 1 corrects Genesis.
fair.note: The Synoptics also contain revelatory material (angelic birth narratives, the Transfiguration, heavenly voices, apocalyptic teaching). John 1 echoes Genesis 1 deliberately, but Christians generally read it as fulfilling or deepening Genesis, not correcting it. Charitable reading: John is widely recognised as the most theologically reflective Gospel.

fair.claim: The axe in Luke 3:9 is aimed at the tree of the knowledge of good and evil and its books.
fair.note: In context the trees are people (or Israel) who fail to bear fruit; the same image appears in Matt 7:19 and Luke 13:6–9. Linking it to Eden’s tree is an allegorical reading peculiar to this series.

fair.claim: The woman at the well was not immoral; certified divorces let unloved women remarry without being stoned for lacking a consummation garment, and a woman could request one.
fair.note: Some scholars do argue she may have been widowed or divorced rather than immoral, since the text never condemns her. But in Jewish law the husband issued the certificate (Deut 24:1); women generally could not initiate divorce. The ‘garment’ law concerned proof of virginity at a first marriage (Deut 22:13–21), not remarriage. In Matt 19 it was Pharisees, not the disciples, who first raised Moses’ certificate, and Jesus calls the hard‑heartedness the husbands’. Samaritans regarded themselves as true Israelites with their own Pentateuch and temple, rather than outsiders wanting to be Jews. Charitable reading: the core point (Jesus does not define her by her past) is widely affirmed.

fair.claim: Mistranslation of Rev 20:15 is blamed on the 1611 King James translators, and the speaker says Greek has only about 17 participles.
fair.note: The rendering “anyone/whosoever” follows the Greek and is in every translation, earlier and later than the KJV. The claim about participles is muddled: Greek has a very rich participle system; the speaker probably meant that pronouns take gender from their referents, which in this verse points to persons.
